item.title: Community fishing locker installed in Hagåtña Mayor’s Office
item.description: The Department of Agriculture’s Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources, or DAWR, and the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office have installed a community fishing locker at the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office. The gear is available to all Guam residents with a valid form of identification. There is no age restriction, and the equipment includes reels sized for children.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Agriculture’s Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources, or DAWR, and the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office have installed a community fishing locker at the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office.

The gear is available to all Guam residents with a valid form of identification. There is no age restriction, and the equipment includes reels sized for children.

The locker has six rod-and-reel combinations in varying sizes, as well as tackle boxes and fishing tackle.

Adults may borrow equipment for themselves or on behalf of a child or guardian.

Borrowers must provide valid identification, complete a Fishing Locker Checkout Form, and sign a participant agreement. After use, the equipment must be returned to the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office for inspection.

DAWR also offers fishing clinics by appointment for community members interested in hands-on fishing instruction.

The Community Fishing Locker was funded through a grant from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Office of Conservation Investment. DAWR says the program aims to make recreational fishing more accessible while encouraging responsible fishing and stewardship of Guam’s aquatic resources.

item.title: Delegate says CNMI must build unemployment system before DUA can launch
item.description: Del. item.content:encoded:
Del. Kimberlyn King‑Hinds said the Commonwealth’s delayed rollout of Disaster Unemployment Assistance is largely due to the CNMI having to build an entirely new administrative system to manage the federally funded program.

Speaking at the Society for Human Resource Management NMI Chapter meeting Wednesday at Pacific Islands Club Saipan, King‑Hinds said the CNMI cannot copy existing unemployment systems used in states because the islands’ economic conditions and workforce structure differ. She said her office is working closely with the Department of Labor to understand the costs, compliance requirements, and long‑term support needed for a CNMI‑specific program.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency has approved more than $10.1 million in DUA for workers who lost jobs or income after Super Typhoon Sinlaku. But without an unemployment insurance platform, the Commonwealth must create new processes for eligibility, payments, and oversight.

King‑Hinds added that federal concerns about fraud — stemming from pandemic‑era unemployment programs — have also slowed implementation. She said the CNMI must design a system that can withstand future disasters and economic downturns, noting that the islands will continue to face typhoons and other shocks.

“This is something we’re building from scratch,” she said.

item.title: Apatang signs FY 2027 budget, issues broad vetoes

item.content:encoded:
CNMI Gov. David M. Apatang on Monday signed Public Law 24‑40, the Fiscal Year 2027 budget, after a five‑day partial government shutdown that began when the administration said it needed additional time to review the Legislature’s spending plan.

In a letter to lawmakers, Apatang said the budget reached his office “just hours prior to the opening of the new fiscal year,” leaving insufficient time for review and prompting the temporary halt in government operations.

The new law sets a projected annual revenue target of about $152.8 million, including $47.7 million in earmarks and $100.7 million allocated across all branches and government instrumentalities.

Apatang approved the overall spending plan but vetoed several provisions he said were unfunded, legally inconsistent, or fiscally unsustainable. He rejected a mandate requiring minimum compensation levels and 64‑hour workweeks, saying the measure would widen the Commonwealth’s budget gap by roughly $3.3 million. He also disapproved of language restricting furloughs and guaranteeing full benefits despite reduced work hours, arguing that agencies must retain flexibility during austerity.

The governor struck a proposed salary cap tied to his July 1 budget submission, calling it a violation of separation of powers. He also vetoed requirements for immediate transfers of FEMA‑reimbursable funds to municipal treasuries, noting that the Department of Finance does not control FEMA drawdowns. Several Public School System funding directives were rejected after Apatang said they front‑loaded spending and created an unfunded mandate of more than $7 million. Additional vetoes affected the Department of Public Lands, the Office of the Attorney General, and other operational provisions he said conflicted with existing law or lacked a sustainable funding source.

Apatang said his administration will implement proportionate budget reductions and forthcoming work‑hour adjustments to align spending with available revenues. With his signature, the budget becomes law and agencies are preparing to resume normal operations.

item.title: Jim Bakker, who built 'PTL Club' televangelism empire, has died at 86
item.description: Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around the hugely successful "The PTL Club" TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86. Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. His cause of death was not immediately clear.
item.content:encoded:
Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around the hugely successful "The PTL Club" TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86.

Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. His cause of death was not immediately clear.

"He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry," she said.

The pair lived near the Missouri entertainment town of Branson and filmed their TV show "The Jim Bakker Show" there since it launched in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020.

But it was another evangelical program that made Jim and his first wife Tammy Faye Bakker cultural icons — so much so that they were often skewered in the 1980s and 1990s by late-night comedians and parodied on "Saturday Night Live." A theatrical movie on their lives, "The Eyes of Tammy Faye," was released in September 2021.

At its peak in the mid-1980s, the Bakkers' ministry included not only the TV show drawing up to 13 million nightly viewers but also the Christian-based Heritage USA theme park and hotel in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and attended North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. They married in 1961 and dropped out of college to start their own traveling ministry — he preached, she sang and played the accordion as they crossed the country visiting churches and tent revivals.

They caught the attention of televangelist Pat Robertson, and in 1965 launched a children's show on Robertson's Christian Broadcasting Network. By 1966, he was hosting "The 700 Club," a Christian talk show.

Bakker left CBN in 1972 and two years later formed the PTL Satellite Network. "The PTL Club" — PTL stands for "Praise the Lord" — became its signature show.

When it hit its heyday in the 1980s, "The PTL Club" was drawing millions of viewers — and bringing in millions of dollars annually from followers.

The show featured chats with guests and Christian entertainers. Bakker offered upbeat sermons and Tammy Faye — charismatic and always wearing her trademark heavy mascara — sang. Most episodes were taped at their sprawling complex just south of Charlotte, North Carolina.

The couple was so famous that they were often parodied by TV comedians for their lavish lifestyle and Tammy Faye's abundant makeup.

In March 1987, their empire began to crack when Bakker admitted to a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Bakker was forced to resign from his own empire, turning over operations to pastor and broadcaster Jerry Falwell.

Tammy Faye stuck by Bakker, often with tears running down her mascara, even as many saw his downfall as a fitting symbol of the greed and hypocrisy of the 1980s.

In 1988, Bakker was indicted for mail fraud, wire fraud and conspiracy after an investigation of PTL's finances. He was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in federal prison, though the sentence was later reduced to eight years.

At a news conference after Bakker was found guilty, Tammy Faye stood in front of the microphones and sang the hymn, "On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand."

Their marriage crumbled and Tammy Faye divorced Bakker in 1992, just short of their 31st anniversary, while he was still in prison. She later married Roe Messner, a building contractor whose projects included the Heritage USA theme park. Messner was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995 and spent about two years in prison.

Tammy Faye died of colon cancer in 2007.

Bakker was released on parole in 1994. He married his second wife, Lori, in 1998. The couple launched "The Jim Bakker Show" on the PTL Satellite Network five years later.

In June 2021, Bakker and his Morningside Church Productions Inc. settled a lawsuit accusing him of falsely claiming the health supplement Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who paid money or gave contributions to obtain the product in the early days of the pandemic.

The lawsuit said Bakker and a guest made the cure claim during 11 episodes in February and March of 2020.

Bakker and Tammy Faye had two children. He and his second wife adopted five children in 2002.

item.title: New York's laws on consent and alcohol use could complicate Cornell case prosecution
item.description: New York Attorney General Letitia James is now in charge of a new investigation into an alleged sexual assault at Cornell University in 2024. LETITIA JAMES: We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions.
item.content:encoded:
New York Attorney General Letitia James is now in charge of a new investigation into an alleged sexual assault at Cornell University in 2024.

LETITIA JAMES: We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions.

CHANG: But pursuing prosecutions could be complicated by the law in New York. We're talking specifically about how New York state law considers alcohol or drug use when determining whether there was consent before sexual contact with another person. We've called up Erin Murphy to explain all of this. She's a professor at NYU School of Law and an expert on sexual assault law. Welcome.

ERIN MURPHY: Thank you. It's good to be here.

CHANG: Good to have you. So can you just briefly explain what New York state law says with respect to the issue of consent in a situation where, say, an accuser has voluntarily consumed drugs or voluntarily consumed alcohol before sexual contact with another individual?

MURPHY: Yeah. So when an individual has voluntarily taken drugs or alcohol and is compromised or impaired, the law requires that the prosecutor prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the person was physically helpless. That's the standard - physical helplessness. And the statute in turn defines that as unconsciousness, so loss of consciousness or a physical incapability to communicate unwillingness. So this...

CHANG: Complete loss of consciousness. So let me just picture this. If an accuser...

CHANG: ...Were, say, semi conscious or barely able to walk, but still able to sort of walk or slurring her speech at the time that an alleged assault happened, would that not be enough to qualify as physical helplessness?

MURPHY: Generally, no. There's a requirement of lack of consciousness. And in fact, sometimes in...

MURPHY: ...Cases, you'll see someone who's passing in and out of consciousness. So they might be, say, vomiting and then back unconscious or kind of - you know, we've all seen someone sort of staggering around or lying, they're moaning. So they're making noises which indicate consciousness, even though we would not think of them as capable of making any kind of decisions. That evidence of just awakeness at any level is often and can be used to show someone is not unconscious and not physically incapable of communication because they are moaning or they are, you know, pushing their hand out or turning their head. The very kind of evidence that you might think shows that someone's not capable of consenting actually shows the contrary under the law of New York, which is - it's someone conscious enough to move to vomit, to, you know, moan, therefore, not unconscious.

CHANG: So in such a case, if someone were going in and out of consciousness, that generally, at least in New York, would not be enough for a prosecutor to bring charges of sexual assault? Is that what you're saying?

MURPHY: It's - yes. There are cases in which...

MURPHY: It's - that's what I would say. It's a very hard case to prove. Now, there are cases where you might have evidence that supports the acts of penetration occurring while someone is unconscious during that, you know, or you might have testimony where someone says, I lost consciousness and, you know, awoke to someone penetrating me. That can support a charge, and a jury can find, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the person was physically helpless.

MURPHY: And, generally, if you have anyone saying, I never lost full consciousness. I was always awake. I just couldn't really articulate words. I couldn't make my body move the way I wanted it to. You know, that kind of incapacitation is not enough.

CHANG: Well, given the requirements under New York state law and what you know about the particular circumstances and alleged facts in the Cornell case, does it seem like it could be a real challenge for Letitia James to bring criminal charges here?

MURPHY: I think we are going to have to see what the investigation uncovered that we're not aware of and what her investigation further uncovers. Often, in cases like these, there might be physical images, digital images, videos. You might have text chains or even people who come into a grand jury and say, you know, I said, oh, didn't - how did that go down? Didn't they - didn't she fight back? And, you know, the answer is, nah, she was so out of it, she didn't even know where she was. That kind of evidence can support even this high standard of physical helplessness. So depending on what comes through in the investigation, there may actually be enough to charge, even at that high strict standard. But more to the point, I think it's important - and this is a moment in time when there's been such a strong public reaction - to reevaluate the laws on the books and, I think, ask, do these laws reflect what we think they should be? Do they set the standard we think appropriate?

CHANG: It's really given way to this huge conversation around these particular requirements under New York state law, so much so that the governor of New York, Kathy Hochul, has said that she would support an update to New York law when it comes to sexual assault. But how likely is it that New York state lawmakers would agree to overhaul this law?

MURPHY: Well, I would hope that they would take this as an opportunity to do just that. This is not the only state in the country that has a restrictive law like this, but there are many other states that have laws that are more protective of victims in this situation that have standards that would recognize that impairment with alcohol or intoxicants to this degree means that an individual cannot give consent.

CHANG: And if New York state lawmakers were to rewrite the law, could it apply retroactively to this Cornell case?

MURPHY: No, any changes in the law would only apply going forward. And, of course, for the victim in this case, that's, you know, cold comfort. But I would hope that at least, if nothing else, she would understand the role that she played in bringing forward change. And although it was not in place to protect or vindicate her own interests and what happened to her, going forward, it would set a new standard that many people would benefit from.

CHANG: Erin Murphy, professor at NYU School of Law. Thank you very much.

MURPHY: Thank you. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

item.title: Is our fate pre-destined? A new 'East of Eden' adaptation asks again

item.content:encoded:
As John Steinbeck wrote it, East of Eden is a sprawling, ambitious, provocative novel, spanning from the Civil War to the end of World War I. Its primary characters include an Irish immigrant family and a Chinese loner, several generations of feuding brothers and an evil and manipulative young girl who matures into an even more evil and manipulative woman. And through it all runs the author's central question: Are we pre-destined to a particular fate and disposition, or can free will overcome?

The movie version, produced in the 1950s and adapted with Steinbeck's input, chopped off the first three-quarters of the book. Director Elia Kazan opens with Cal Trask, one of two very dissimilar brothers, hunting down his mother, who abandoned the family right after her twins were born. Cal and his brother, Aron, are like the biblical Cain and Abel — one is good by nature, the other evil — but in the movie, Cal is played with palpable charisma by James Dean.

The next version of East of Eden arrived in 1981. The six-hour ABC miniseries used the extra time to include more characters and stories neglected in the film. The Hamiltons, the Irish family, are given lots of room to develop, as is Lee, the Chinese caretaker, who is much wiser than he originally appears. Most of all, that miniseries brought the character of Cathy to dead center. As played by Jane Seymour , she was a force of nature — and of pure evil, who, after giving birth to twins she didn't want, would shoot her husband and abandon her babies.

I've revisited these earlier versions to put into a fuller context just what Zoe Kazan has done in revising, and remaking, the story first brought to screen by her grandfather. This new Netflix miniseries, at about seven hours, is slightly longer than the older one — but it basically eliminates the Irish American family, so it can't claim to be more complete. It also can't claim to be the first to focus on the feminist perspective, because the ABC version certainly did that. The new version, though, explores even more fully the transition of Cathy, the young girl, to Kate, the prostitute.

Florence Pugh , as Kate, is given more justification for her actions. She's also given more voice: Instead of Steinbeck providing narration about Kate and her childhood, this new East of Eden has Kate supply it herself. Which she does while listening to a lecture by the man she's about to target.

Pugh's portrayal of Kate, even at the end, is more glamorous than in the previous versions, which showed Kate as older and arthritic. But the drama is unchanged, and many of the confrontation scenes, even ones without violence, are uncomfortably intense. Netflix allows for more sex scenes and nudity, so there's lots of both. But most of these are staged as almost the opposite of erotic: either matter-of-factly, or with one or both parties taking part unwillingly or unenthusiastically. On the night Cathy marries her husband Adam, played by Christopher Abbott, she leaves his bed, and slips into the next room — and into the bed of Adam's brother, Charles, who's understandably startled.

Pugh, like Seymour before her, deserves the spotlight here, and fills it. But watch, also, for Hoon Lee as the family's Chinese manservant and Martha Plimpton as Kate's madam. They're excellent, too. And best of all, this new East of Eden hammers home Steinbeck's primary theme — and suggests, after all the deaths and misery, a potentially happy ending.

item.title: Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at age 84

item.content:encoded:
Dennis Hastert, whose political legacy as Congress' longest-serving Republican House speaker was later fouled by allegations that he had molested high school athletes during his prior career as a teacher and wrestling coach, has died, a coroner said Monday. He was 84.

Hastert, who was speaker from 1999 until 2007, died Saturday of natural causes at his home while receiving hospice care, according to Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell.

When he was sentenced in 2016 to more than a year behind bars, the former history teacher became one of the highest-ranking American politicians ever ordered to prison.

In the late 1990s, Hastert was a little-known Illinois lawmaker with a reputation for congeniality that had helped him ascend the ranks of congressional leaders. When Newt Gingrich lost support because of ethics violations and the GOP's poor showing in an election, Republicans elected Hastert to succeed him. In his first weeks on the job, he presided over the House while the Senate conducted then-President Bill Clinton's impeachment trial.

After the GOP reclaimed the White House, Hastert helped pass then-President George W. Bush's legislative agenda, including massive tax cuts and a measure that amounted to a huge expansion of prescription drug benefits — the biggest change in Medicare in decades.

His legacy was suddenly thrown into doubt in 2015, when he was accused of evading banking regulations as part of a plan to pay hush money to conceal unspecified "prior misconduct." Nearly a year later, prosecutors filed papers that described what media reports had suggested for months: Hastert's alleged misconduct involved the sexual abuse of teenage boys on his wrestling team in the small town of Yorkville, west of Chicago.

During a 16-year coaching career, he led his team to a state championship and was named national coach of the year in 1976. But behind the accolades, prosecutors said, Hastert sexually abused at least four team members from 1965 to 1981.

The person Hastert was paying, identified in court papers only as Individual A, said the abuse occurred in a motel room when he was 14 on the way home from wrestling camp. Hastert allegedly touched other wrestlers in a locker room after saying he would give them massages. Two wrestlers said Hastert performed sexual acts on them.

Prosecutors also described a recliner where Hastert often sat in the locker room with a direct view of the stalls where the boys showered.

Hastert agreed to plead guilty to evading banking laws. In all, he paid more than $1.7 million out of $3.5 million that he had promised to Individual A, sometimes in lump sums of $100,000 cash.

At the sentencing hearing where he received 15 months behind bars, the visibly angry judge called Hastert a "serial child molester." A former wrestler struggled with his emotions as he told the court about his "dark secret" from adolescence.

In his own statement, Hastert said he was "deeply ashamed" and admitted that he "mistreated" some of his athletes. But he never referred directly to sexual abuse.

The public knew nothing about Hastert's past when Republicans lost seats in the 1998 midterm elections.

Hastert's path to the speaker's office was cleared when Louisiana Rep. Bob Livingston, who was considered a lock to replace Gingrich as speaker, resigned after acknowledging several extramarital affairs.

Hastert was aware of the personal pitfalls of holding the powerful position.

"You know, in this business, especially in a job like this, you can get your head someplace where it shouldn't be," Hastert said in a 1999 interview with The Associated Press. "But you come back home, and you're home. You're back where you've always been, and your feet are back on the ground."

Hastert said he lacked the appetite for higher office.

As the recount of the 2000 presidential election dragged on, Hastert's aides briefed him on the possibility that he might become acting president in the event of an Electoral College deadlock.

"I really didn't want to be president, temporary or otherwise," he wrote in his book. But he decided that he would not pass the office to the constitutional officer next in line if an Electoral College deadlock extended beyond Inauguration Day. In the end, the Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling ended the recount, and Bush moved into the White House.

Hastert's journey to Congress from his boyhood farm appeared to be the result of fate and luck.

In 1980, he finished third in an Illinois House primary. But the incumbent became fatally ill, and GOP leaders chose Hastert to take his place on the November ballot, where he won in a traditional GOP stronghold.

Hastert became a congressional candidate in 1986 and beat the Democrat with 52% of the vote, his smallest margin of victory in a congressional race.

In Washington, Hastert served quietly in House leadership, working closely with Gingrich and then-House Majority Whip Tom DeLay after Republicans took control in 1995.

Hastert became wealthy largely through a complex web of transactions that coincided with one of his own highway earmarks increasing the value of land he had purchased in his district.

He was forced to step down as speaker in 2007, when Democrats gained control of the House, and he resigned his seat later that year.

Born in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert earned a bachelor's degree in economics from Wheaton College in 1964 and a master's in education from Northern Illinois University in 1967.

In 2007, Wheaton named its newly created public policy center the J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government and Public Policy. After Hastert's indictment, the school removed his name in 2015. Other organizations abandoned associations with Hastert, and his portrait was removed from a hallway outside the House chamber.

Hastert lived his entire life in Chicago's suburbs, primarily in the Yorkville area. While growing up, he helped his father with the family feed business.

Survivors include his wife, Jean, and two adult sons.
